Six records, in the order they happened

The shelf, not the highlight reel — each record opened for its story, its personnel, and the thing that nearly stopped it.

The man at the piano

First person, because a booking is a person before it is a band.

I learned piano the way a lot of Tremé kids did — at my grandmother’s church, standing on the bench to reach the pedals, playing hymns by ear before I could read a note. The choir director, Miss Odette, charged me nothing and forgave me less. Every voicing I play still answers to her.

At twenty-one I took a Thursday residency at a Frenchmen Street club: four sets a night, tips in a brandy snifter, a house piano that lost its middle C every time the humidity rose. I played that room for six years. It taught me the only lesson that matters on a bandstand — the audience is not a crowd, it is a conversation, and you do not get to be boring in a conversation.

Since then: nine albums, twelve film scores, and a lot of borrowed pianos. I write at a desk in the Marigny with the windows open, I still take the church gig at Christmas, and I still believe a trio that listens is worth more than an orchestra that doesn’t. Book me and you get the same man the records got — no substitutes, no tracks, no phoning it in.

What the room says afterwards

JC
“Elias has played my room for nineteen years, and I will tell you the whole secret: he never once played down to it. Wedding party, slow Tuesday, festival crowd bleeding in off the street — same man, same weight on the keys. Rooms don’t have regulars. Pianists like him are why they do.”
June CallowayOwner · The Lantern, Frenchmen Street · New Orleans
MW
“He watched the cut once, in silence, then sat down and played the river the way it actually sounds at 5 a.m. I rewrote my ending around his theme. Directors say that about composers all the time. It was true exactly once.”
Marcus WebbDocumentary director · The Levee Line
AG
“He learned my father’s song — a tune nobody had written down — from a cassette my mother described over the phone. At the wedding he played it once, plainly, and my father stood up and sang. Book the trio. Then thank me.”
Althea GrantMarried at the Marigny Opera House · 2023

Asked at the bar, most nights

Do you play outside New Orleans?

Gladly — festivals and scores take him across the South and further. Travel and lodging are added at cost, never marked up, and the calculator’s range already assumes a New Orleans room; ask and he will quote the trip honestly.

What piano do you need?

A grand that was tuned this season is his first love. If the room has no piano, his stage piano travels with him and is delivered, set and collected by his own crew — it is in the quote, not on top of it.

Can you play our song?

Send it a month ahead and he will arrange it himself — a cassette description over the phone has worked before now. Requests on the night are welcomed too; if he doesn’t know it, he will tell you plainly and play you something better.

How far ahead do evenings book?

Clubs usually two to three months out, weddings and festival stages four to six. The chip at the top of this page is computed from his real book — if it names a month, that month genuinely has evenings left.

How does booking work?

A short call, a one-page agreement, and a 30% deposit hold your date. The balance is due on the night. No agents and no management company — the man who answers is the man who plays.
